title: The 5 Rarest Main Blood Types, Ranked (Universal Donor Is Only #5)

scenes.text: The five rarest of the eight main blood types. The one every hospital wants is only fifth.

scenes.label: O negative · 6.6%
scenes.text: Number five: O negative, about 6.6 percent of Americans. The universal donor. In an emergency, its red cells can go to anyone.

scenes.label: A negative · 6.3%
scenes.text: Number four: A negative, about 6.3 percent. Roughly one person in sixteen.

scenes.label: AB positive · 3.4%
scenes.text: Number three: AB positive, about 3.4 percent. The universal recipient: it can take red cells from every other type.

scenes.label: B negative · 1.5%
scenes.text: Number two: B negative, about 1.5 percent. One person in sixty-seven.

scenes.label: AB negative · 0.6%
scenes.text: Number one: AB negative. About 0.6 percent, one American in 170. The rarest blood of the eight, and yet its plasma can be given to anyone.

description:
The five rarest of the eight main blood types in the United States, ranked by share of the population.
Using Stanford Blood Center figures: O negative about 6.6 percent, A negative 6.3, AB positive 3.4, B negative 1.5 and AB negative just 0.6. O negative red cells can be given to any patient, AB positive patients can receive red cells from any type, and AB plasma is the universal plasma. Shares differ between countries and ethnic groups, and far rarer types exist outside the main eight.
Do you know your own blood type?
first_comment: The most common type, O positive, is in about 37 percent of Americans. Which type are you, and what should we rank next?
